title: Explainer: Charter Revision Commissions Appointed by Prior Mayors
plain_title: What a mayor can do about a prior mayor's charter commission
what_they_audited: A question-and-answer explainer by Citizens Union and Reinvent Albany, two good-government groups, on charter revision commissions appointed by a mayor on the way out of office. It was prompted by the commission former Mayor Adams established on December 31, 2025.
background: Section 36 of the New York Municipal Home Rule Law gives mayors, city councils and voters the power to create a charter commission and sets how commissions place questions on the ballot. A charter commission can block, or bump, ballot questions submitted by the City Council or by voter initiative.

findings.plain: State law, not the New York City Charter, governs how charter revision commissions are created and how they put questions before voters.
The groups write that the State Legislature and the governor could amend the Municipal Home Rule Law to deal with commissions appointed by a departing mayor, including commissions that already exist.
findings.quote: we believe that the Legislature and Governor can amend the Municipal Home Rule

findings.plain: On whether a sitting mayor can remove commissioners appointed by a predecessor, the Q&A concludes it might be possible in some cases but would likely be settled in court.
findings.quote: POTENTIALLY IN SOME CASES, BUT IT WOULD BE INADVISABLE

findings.plain: State law does let a sitting mayor fill any vacancy on a commission that a previous mayor appointed.
findings.quote: shall be filled by the mayor

findings.plain: Nothing in the law requires a mayor to fund or support a commission created by a predecessor, so a commission can be left without money, space, legal advice or data.
findings.quote: The law allows a mayor to “starve” a mayoral charter commission of government resources,

findings.plain: A commission is not required to propose any ballot questions, yet its existence alone can block questions put forward by the City Council or by voters.
findings.quote: The mere existence of a mayoral charter revision commission introduces the threat that it

findings.plain: Whether a charter commission may accept private donations is unsettled, and the Office of Management and Budget has discretion over city agency bank accounts.
findings.quote: It is unclear how this section applies in the context of private contributions.

numbers.label: Window a proposed state amendment would give a new mayor
Donations to agencies reported yearly to the ethics board

recommendations: Amend the state Municipal Home Rule Law so that a charter revision commission appointed in the last six months of a mayor's term must be affirmed by the incoming mayor within 90 days or dissolve.

Do not attempt to remove charter commissioners appointed by a previous mayor without cause, which the groups say would open the door to routine political purges of bodies that have operated independently.
Consider using an executive order to bar direct donations to mayoral charter revision commissions and the creation of affiliated nonprofits to raise money for them.
